extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets and dramatists (writers of verse and stage-plays)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and aesthetic guidance for composing poetry and drama: choosing subjects, arranging parts, diction, genre decorum, characterization, and stage-craft so a work both delights and instructs. Focus is on poets/playwrights aiming for polished, effective verse for public performance or reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a subject suitable to your abilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Ye who write, make choice of a subject suitable to your abilities; and revolve in your thoughts a considerable time what your strength declines, and what it is able to support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select topics you can handle well rather than overreach. Consider personal strength and limit; a judicious choice preserves elegance and perspicuity. Avoid subjects that demand skills you lack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and unity of subject
rubrics_metrics.description: In a word, be your subject what it will, let it be merely simple and uniform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid patchwork, over-ambitious mixtures or subject-hopping (likened to a picture with mismatched parts). Keep a single coherent focus rather than fusing incongruous elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement: say what ought just now to be said
rubrics_metrics.description: This, or I am mistaken, will constitute the merit and beauty of arrangement, that the poet just now say what ought just now to be said, put off most of his thoughts, and waive them for the present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order material so each moment contains what is timely and necessary; omit or postpone digressions. Good pacing and placement are central to effective structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction: choose words delicately and cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: In the choice of his words, too, the author of the projected poem must be delicate and cautious, he must embrace one and reject another: you will express yourself eminently well, if a dexterous combination should give an air of novelty to a well-known word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be selective with vocabulary; prefer clarity and aptness. A novel phrasing of an old word can be effective, but avoid awkward coinages unless modestly justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted coinage and Greek derivation
rubrics_metrics.description: If it happen to be necessary to explain some abstruse subjects by new invented terms; it will follow that you must frame words never heard of by the old-fashioned Cethegi: and the license will be granted, if modestly used: and the new and lately-formed words will have authority, if they descend from a Greek source, with a slight deviation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coin new words sparingly and modestly; Greek-based innovations are more acceptable. Let custom be the final arbiter of language's acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixing incompatible elements (decorum of style)
rubrics_metrics.description: We are conscious of this, and this privilege we demand and allow in turn: but not to such a degree, that the tame should associate with the savage; nor that serpents should be coupled with birds, lambs with tigers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain stylistic consistency; don't combine incompatible tones, images, or registers that strain credibility or taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain genre propriety (tragic/comic decorum)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic subject will not be handled in tragic verse: in like manner the banquet of Thyestes will not bear to be held in familiar verses, and such as almost suit the sock. Let each peculiar species [of writing] fill with decorum its proper place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect conventions of genre and metric forms. If blending occurs, do so with care and a clear artistic purpose to avoid discordance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bombast and obscurity; aim for skillful balance
rubrics_metrics.description: I labor to be concise, I become obscure: nerves and spirit fail him, that aims at the easy: one, that pretends to be sublime, proves bombastical: he who is too cautious and fearful of the storm, crawls along the ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strike a balance between plainness and sublimity. Do not sacrifice clarity for attempted grandeur, nor prefer safety to the point of lifelessness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: If you offer to the stage any thing unattempted, and venture to form a new character; let it be preserved to the last such as it set out at the beginning, and be consistent with itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New or invented characters must remain psychologically consistent throughout; avoid arbitrary changes that break verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give each character language and manners fitting age and station
rubrics_metrics.description: It will make a wide difference, whether it be Davus that speaks, or a hero; a man well-stricken in years, or a hot young fellow in his bloom; and a matron of distinction, or an officious nurse; ... That the parts [therefore] belonging to age may not be given to youth, and those of a man to a boy, we must dwell upon those qualities which are joined and adapted to each person's age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor diction, behavior and concerns to the character's social rank and stage of life for authenticity and decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke genuine emotion (pathos must be sincere)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not enough that poems be beautiful; let them be tender and affecting, and bear away the soul of the auditor whithersoever they please. As the human countenance smiles on those that smile, so does it sympathize with those that weep. If you would have me weep you must first express the passion of grief yourself...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey passions convincingly: the writer must feel and express the emotion before the audience will be moved. Avoid artificial or performed sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not show what should be offstage (respect theatrical plausibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: You must not, however, bring upon the stage things fit only to be acted behind the scenes: and you must take away from view many actions, which elegant description may soon after deliver in presence [of the spectators]. Let not Medea murder her sons before the people; nor the execrable Atreus openly dress human entrails: nor let Progue be metamorphosed into a bird, Cadmus into a serpent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep horrific, unbelievable, or implausible actions offstage and communicate them via description or narration to preserve audience belief and decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not demand belief for absurdities
rubrics_metrics.description: Let what ever is imagined for the sake of entertainment, have as much likeness to truth as possible; let not your play demand belief for whatever [absurdities] it is inclinable [to exhibit]: nor take out of a witch's belly a living child that she had dined upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure fictional elements remain plausible within the work's internal logic; avoid implausible spectacles that break suspension of disbelief.

rubrics_metrics.name: On innovation: alter the known with taste and omit what you cannot polish
rubrics_metrics.description: He always hastens on to the event; and hurries away his reader in the midst of interesting circumstances, no otherwise than as if they were [already] known; and what he despairs of, as to receiving a polish from his touch, he omits; and in such a manner forms his fictions, so intermingles the false with the true, that the middle is not inconsistent with the beginning, nor the end with the middle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innovate by selection and compression: omit parts you cannot finish well, mix invention and tradition so the whole remains consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep a play to appropriate length and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a play which would be inquired after, and though seen, represented anew, be neither shorter nor longer than the fifth act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect traditional act-structure and proportion (here: five acts). Avoid arbitrary truncation or overextension that harms dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit divine intervention to serious necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither let a god interfere, unless a difficulty worthy a god's unraveling should happen;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve supernatural deus ex machina only for problems that truly require divine resolution; don't use gods as lazy plot-fixers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus must be coherent and relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the chorus sustain the part and manly character of an actor: nor let them sing any thing between the acts which is not conducive to, and fitly coherent with, the main design. Let them both patronize the good, and give them friendly advice, and regulate the passionate...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the chorus to support theme and action, advise, praise virtue, and maintain coherence with the play's main design; avoid irrelevant interludes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical accompaniment should be modest and appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The flute, ... slender and of simple form, with few stops, was of service to accompany and assist the chorus ... But when the victorious Romans began to extend their territories ... the musician added now movements and a luxuriance to the ancient art, and strutting backward and forward, drew a length of train over the stage; thus likewise new notes were added ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simple, supportive accompaniment that suits the mood and audience. Avoid ostentatious musical or stage excess that distracts or cheapens the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match tone to speaker: pathetic for sorrow, menace for anger, etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Pathetic accents suit a melancholy countenance; words full of menace, an angry one; wanton expressions, a sportive look; and serious matter, an austere one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure verbal tone aligns with the character's emotion and physical bearing; mismatch leads to audience laughter or disbelief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study models but avoid slavish literal translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ye [who are desirous to excel,] turn over the Grecian models by night, turn them by day. ... nor must you be so faithful a translator, as to take the pains of rendering [the original] word for word; nor by imitating throw yourself into straits, whence either shame or the rules of your work may forbid you to retreat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn from Greek models extensively, but adapt rather than translate word-for-word. Preserve spirit over literal wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good sense (common sense about life and duties) is the first principle
rubrics_metrics.description: To have good sense, is the first principle and fountain of writing well. The Socratic papers will direct you in the choice of your subjects; and words will spontaneously accompany the subject, when it is well conceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground works in sound moral and social understanding: knowledge of human duties, offices, and manners produces apt characterizations and situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness in precepts and writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever precepts you give, be concise; that docile minds may soon comprehend what is said, and faithfully retain it. All superfluous instructions flow from the too full memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be succinct in instruction and expression; eliminate superfluity so readers/listeners retain and are edified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write to both instruct and delight (utile et dulce)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets wish either to profit or to delight; or to deliver at once both the pleasures and the necessaries of life. He who joins the instructive with the agreeable, carries off every vote, by delighting and at the same time admonishing the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to teach and entertain simultaneously; an effective poem or play combines moral or useful content with pleasurable form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metric and rhythmic propriety (avoid awkward spondees in trimeters)
rubrics_metrics.description: A long syllable put after a short one is termed an iambus ... it obligingly and contentedly admitted into its paternal heritage the steadfast spondees; agreeing however, by social league, that it was not to depart from the second and fourth place. But this [kind of measure] rarely makes its appearance in the notable trimeters of Accius, and brands the verse of Ennius ... with a clumsy weight of spondees, with the imputation of being too precipitate and careless, or disgracefully accuses him of ignorance in his art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe metrical norms of the chosen form. Excessive or ill-placed spondees/irregularities create heaviness or reveal ineptitude; aim for ear-pleasing cadence and correct placement of feet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid offensive or obscene speech that alienates respectable audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: For [at such stuff] all are offended, who have a horse, a father, or an estate: nor will they receive with approbation, nor give the laurel crown, as the purchasers of parched peas and nuts are delighted with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from indecent or scandalous remarks that alienate respectable segments of the audience; coarse humour has limits depending on public taste.
